subject: Mixed
description: Hard-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Biochemistry, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, General Surgery & Orthopedics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Pharmacology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychology.

questions.question: The physiological relaxation of the pelvic joints (symphysis pubis and sacroiliac joints) during pregnancy is primarily attributed to which hormones?

options.B: Insulin and glucagon
options.C: Thyroxine only
options.D: Adrenaline and cortisol

questions.explanation: Relaxation of the pelvic joints during pregnancy — increased width and mobility of the symphysis pubis, and similar changes in the sacroiliac joints — is attributed to the hormones progesterone and relaxin, facilitating the anteroposterior diameter increase needed during labor.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Fetal Skull and Maternal Pelvis — Physiological Enlargement of Pelvis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Within the femoral sheath, which compartment contains the femoral canal (occupied by a lymph node), and which structure occupies the intermediate compartment?

options.A: The medial compartment is the femoral canal; the femoral vein occupies the intermediate compartment
options.B: The lateral compartment is the femoral canal; the femoral artery occupies the intermediate compartment
options.C: The femoral nerve occupies the femoral canal
options.D: There is only one compartment in the femoral sheath

questions.explanation: The femoral sheath has three compartments: the lateral compartment contains the femoral artery, the intermediate compartment contains the femoral vein, and the medial compartment is the femoral canal, occupied by a lymph node (and providing space for femoral vein distension, and the path for femoral hernias).
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Lower Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Front of Thigh — Femoral Triangle
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) is used to assess for which type of knee instability?

options.B: Posterolateral rotary instability
options.C: Isolated medial collateral ligament sprain only
options.D: Patellofemoral instability

questions.explanation: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) tests for posterolateral rotary instability — a positive test (jerk in the knee, or posterior tibial shift with a 'giving way' sensation) indicates injury to the lateral collateral ligament, arcuate-popliteus complex, and mid-third of the lateral capsule.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Posterolateral Rotary Instability
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: Morning headaches in a patient with severe respiratory failure may signify:

options.B: Simple dehydration only
options.C: Normal sleep patterns with no pathology
options.D: Acute pulmonary embolism specifically

questions.explanation: Morning headaches in patients with severe respiratory failure may signify nocturnal carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia during sleep), which can be confirmed with early morning arterial blood gases or nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Pronase is distinct from enzymes like trypsin or chymotrypsin in protein chemistry because it:

options.A: Is a single enzyme with very narrow specificity for one bond
options.B: Is a mixture of non-specific proteolytic enzymes that causes complete hydrolysis of a protein down to free amino acids
options.C: Only cleaves carbohydrate-protein bonds in glycoproteins
options.D: Cannot hydrolyse peptide bonds at all

questions.explanation: Pronase is a mixture of non-specific proteolytic enzymes that, unlike the more selective trypsin/chymotrypsin/pepsin/elastase, causes complete hydrolysis of a protein all the way down to its free amino acids — useful for determining total amino acid composition rather than sequence.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: When you move your head, objects nearer than your fixation point appear to move in the OPPOSITE direction to your head movement, while objects farther than the fixation point move in the SAME direction. This is the depth cue of:

options.B: Interposition
options.C: Linear perspective
options.D: Gradient of texture

questions.explanation: This is the movement (motion parallax) cue for depth: objects closer than the fixation point appear to move opposite to head movement, while objects farther than the fixation point move in the same direction — and the amount of apparent movement is smaller for distant objects than for near ones.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Sensory Processes and Perception — Monocular Cues for Depth Perception
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: PLP-dependent decarboxylation of glutamate produces which inhibitory neurotransmitter?

options.B: Serotonin
options.C: Histamine
options.D: Dopamine

questions.explanation: Glutamate undergoes PLP-dependent decarboxylation to form GABA (gamma-amino butyric acid), which inhibits nerve impulse transmission and is therefore classified as an inhibitory neurotransmitter — distinct from serotonin (from tryptophan) and histamine (from histidine), which are also PLP-dependent decarboxylation products but are not GABA.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Vitamins — Vitamin B6, Decarboxylation
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: Why is a scaphoid fracture through the waist of the bone at particular risk of avascular necrosis?

options.A: The scaphoid has no nutrient artery at all
options.B: Both nutrient arteries typically enter through the distal part (tubercle/body), so a waist fracture can cut off blood supply to the proximal fragment
options.C: The scaphoid is the only carpal bone with no cartilage covering
options.D: Scaphoid fractures always damage the ulnar nerve directly

questions.explanation: The scaphoid's blood supply normally enters via nutrient arteries at the tubercle (palmar surface) and the dorsal surface of the body — both relatively distal. A waist fracture can therefore deprive the proximal fragment of its blood supply, since retrograde flow to that fragment is often insufficient, leading to avascular necrosis and a high risk of nonunion.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: In managing spasticity in MS patients, why must a therapist be cautious about excessive pharmacological reduction of spasticity in some patients?

options.A: Spasticity has no functional role and should always be eliminated completely
options.B: Spasticity can sometimes be functionally useful (e.g. extensor spasticity assisting standing during a stand-pivot transfer), so over-reducing it may cause loss of function
options.C: Antispasticity medications have no side effects to worry about
options.D: Spasticity always improves function no matter how severe

questions.explanation: While excessive spasticity impairs function, spasticity can sometimes substitute for lost strength — for example, extensor spasticity assisting a patient during a stand-pivot transfer. Significant pharmacological reduction of spasticity in such cases could therefore paradoxically worsen functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 16: Multiple Sclerosis — Management of Symptoms, Spasticity
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: In a patient with acute respiratory distress and suspected pulmonary embolism, what is the significance of a completely NORMAL chest radiograph?

options.B: A normal radiograph does NOT exclude a major pulmonary embolus — in fact, a normal film in a patient with acute respiratory distress is actually suggestive of the diagnosis
options.C: It means the patient definitely has pneumonia instead
options.D: It has no diagnostic relevance whatsoever

questions.explanation: A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude a major pulmonary embolus. In fact, in a patient presenting with acute respiratory distress, a normal-appearing radiograph is actually suggestive of pulmonary embolism as the underlying diagnosis, since conventional radiographic findings in PE are nonspecific (or absent).
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Pulmonary Embolism
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: A clinician decides to keep a patient in hospital 'just in case', despite evidence-based guidelines and a completed systematic assessment supporting discharge, because they recently encountered a similar rare case. This is an example of which cognitive bias?

options.B: Availability bias
options.C: Commission bias only, unrelated to availability
options.D: The framing effect exclusively

questions.explanation: Availability bias occurs when a recent or memorable case distorts a clinician's estimate of probability, making a rare condition seem more likely simply because it is 'at the forefront of the mind' — exactly as described, overriding a systematic (Type 2) assessment with an irrational intuitive override.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Common Cognitive Biases
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: True phimosis, as distinguished from a normal non-retractile foreskin in a young boy, is characterised by:

options.A: Simple inability to retract the foreskin at age 2, which is entirely normal
options.B: Whitish scarring of the foreskin caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), rarely seen before age 5
options.C: Ballooning of the foreskin during urination with no scarring
options.D: A condition that always requires surgery in infancy

questions.explanation: 'Phimosis' is often wrongly applied to a normal non-retractile foreskin, which is common and physiological in young boys. True phimosis is pathological whitish scarring caused by balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), and is rare before 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Foreskin and Circumcision
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: A hallmark intellectual deficit seen after prefrontal-lobe damage, distinct from a general drop in IQ (which is often unaffected), is:

options.A: Complete loss of the ability to speak
options.B: Difficulty planning and sequencing actions, plus perseveration (continuing a behaviour even when the situation demands a new response)
options.C: Total inability to recognize faces
options.D: Immediate loss of all long-term memories formed before the injury

questions.explanation: While standard IQ tests are often little affected by prefrontal damage, patients show subtle but characteristic deficits: difficulty planning a sequence of actions, and perseveration — a tendency to keep behaving the same way even when circumstances call for a different response.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Frontal-Lobe Association Cortex
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Why is the metaphysis of a growing long bone especially important clinically when it lies partly within a joint capsule?

options.A: It has no blood supply, so infection cannot spread there at all
options.B: Being an actively growing, richly vascularised part of the bone, infection there can spread into the joint if the metaphysis is intracapsular (and vice versa)
options.C: It is always extracapsular in every long bone, so it never affects joints
options.D: It only matters in the lower limb, not the upper limb

questions.explanation: The metaphysis is the actively growing part of the bone adjacent to the epiphyseal line, with a rich blood supply — making it a common site for infection in young people. Where the metaphysis is partly or wholly intracapsular (as at the upper end of the humerus), joint infection can spread to the metaphysis, and metaphyseal disease can spread into the joint.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Capsular Attachments and Epiphyseal Lines
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Plasmodium falciparum causes markedly more severe (malignant) malaria than the other three plasmodial species mainly because:

options.A: It has an exo-erythrocytic stage that the others lack
options.B: It only infects the liver, never red blood cells
options.C: It parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell multiple times, and makes parasitised red cells sticky, causing capillary obstruction in deep organs
options.D: It is transmitted by a different mosquito genus entirely

questions.explanation: Unlike the other plasmodial species (which parasitise only juvenile red cells and lack these features), P. falciparum parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell with more than one parasite, and makes infected red cells sticky — causing capillary obstruction (e.g. in the brain, producing cerebral malaria) that accounts for its exceptional virulence. It also notably lacks an exo-erythrocytic stage, but that is not the source of its severity.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: When naming a peptide, the amino acid suffixes (e.g. '-ine' in glycine) are changed to '-yl' for every residue EXCEPT which one?

options.B: The C-terminal residue
options.C: Any residue in the middle of the chain
options.D: Cysteine specifically, regardless of position

questions.explanation: In peptide nomenclature, every amino acid's suffix is changed to '-yl' except the C-terminal residue, which keeps its normal name. For example, a tripeptide of glutamate-cysteine-glycine (glycine being C-terminal) is named glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: The 'ceiling effect' of manual muscle testing refers to which limitation of the technique?

options.A: It cannot detect any degree of weakness whatsoever
options.B: A wide range of actual muscle force can all be labeled Grade 5 (Normal), masking real strength differences among people graded 'normal'
options.C: It systematically overestimates weakness in older adults
options.D: It is not valid for testing lower-extremity muscles

questions.explanation: Studies comparing MMT to hand-held dynamometry found knee extension forces ranging roughly from 85 to over 800 Newtons all classified as Grade 5 (Normal) by break testing. This 'ceiling effect' means MMT loses the ability to distinguish real strength differences once a muscle is already strong, so it is not recommended as a measure of progress above Grade 3.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 2: Relevance and Limitations of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: The (modified) Wells score is a clinical prediction rule used to estimate pre-test probability for which condition?

options.B: Pulmonary embolism / deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Community-acquired pneumonia severity
options.D: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation

questions.explanation: The Wells score is a clinical prediction rule used to estimate the pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism (and, in another version, deep vein thrombosis), helping guide which further tests (e.g. D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiogram) are appropriate.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Clinical Prediction Rules
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: While a rising current initiates an impulse most effectively at the cathode, a FALL in current (when it occurs) is more effective at initiating an impulse at which electrode?

options.B: The anode
options.C: Neither electrode is affected by a falling current
options.D: Both electrodes equally

questions.explanation: A fall in current is less effective overall at initiating an impulse than a rise, but when it does have an effect, it is the anode side of the nerve that is affected — so the anode produces greater stimulation than the cathode specifically in response to a falling current, the reverse of the pattern seen with a rising current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: In anaphylactic shock from drug hypersensitivity, what is described as the only truly life-saving measure?

options.B: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine)
options.C: Oral prednisolone alone
options.D: Waiting for spontaneous resolution

questions.explanation: Intramuscular adrenaline is the only life-saving measure in anaphylactic shock or laryngeal angioedema, repeated every 5-10 minutes if needed. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids have adjuvant value (glucocorticoids act slowly but help with prolonged/severe reactions) but are not substitutes for adrenaline.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Treatment of Drug Allergy
questions.subject: Pharmacology
